The fourth confuses a mark of uninterest with a preference, and a system optimising for time would treat that mark as a signal to change, not as a promotion. A useful habit is to ask what the reader would have to do for the ranking to change.
questions.hint: Ask which quantity a reader would have to change to move a post, and whether that is the one named in the claim.

questions.stem: Der Auszug wird an «separate what a shared wireless network exposes from what a padlock or a second factor protects / Ask who stands between the…» geprüt. Welche Antwort bleibt bestehen?

options.text: The traffic can be read by whoever is on the same network

options.misconception: conflates an encrypted link to the bank with an encrypted link to the router

options.text: The café is legally responsible for whatever the browser sends to the bank

questions.explanation: What a shared wireless network exposes is the link between the device and the access point, because a radio signal is readable by anyone in range who knows how. Traffic that is sent without additional protection is therefore visible to the other people in the café, and a virtual private network is the usual remedy because it moves the trust to a single encrypted tunnel. The padlock in the address bar is a genuine guarantee, but it guarantees only the leg from the device to the bank, and a learner who reads it as covering the whole chain has already lost the point. The third option confuses two different responsibilities: owning the router does not make a café answer for what a guest sends. The fourth is wrong because a cable removes the radio leg entirely, and the exposure that remains is much smaller. The useful habit is to ask, for every connection, who is standing between me and the other end, and then to notice that a VPN is a way of naming one intermediate party and trusting it deliberately.
questions.hint: Ask who stands between the device and the bank on each kind of connection.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: How a false claim keeps spreading
questions.learningObjective: describe the mechanism that keeps a false claim circulating and why correction does not stop it

stimulus.body: In einer Arbeitsnotiz zu diesem Punkt heißt es: Vier Aussagen werden angeboten; nur eine wird durch den Text tatsächlich gestützt.

questions.stem: Wendet man «describe the mechanism that keeps a false claim circulating and why correction does not stop it / Ask what the sender pays to…» auf den Text an, welche Option ist begründet?

answer.exemplar: The mechanism is repetition. A claim that has been seen is more readily believed the second time and more readily passed on, and a repetition arriving from somebody known is harder to check than one arriving from a stranger. Repetition is also cheap for the sender and expensive to answer, since a correction has to be produced, distributed and then believed against the original. That is why an official denial published once loses to a claim repeated a hundred times. Correcting does not always stop it, for four reasons. The correction travels along the same network as the claim but usually with less energy, because few people forward a correction who would have forwarded the claim. A reader who has already repeated the claim has a stake in it and treats the correction as an attack on that. The correction is normally read as a competing claim about the same event rather than as an answer to the particular version the reader saw. And the correction, however accurate, is shorter and duller than the claim, so it loses the competition for attention. What does work is repetition of the correction in the same channels and in the same format, which is why fact-checking services are publications rather than one-off statements.

questions.explanation: The mechanism is repetition, and it has two halves that are usually run together. The first is that a claim which has already been seen is more readily believed the next time and more readily passed on, so the belief is produced by the exposure rather than by the content. The second is that forwarding is cheap for the sender and answering is expensive, since a correction has to be written, distributed and then believed against something the reader has already forwarded. The second half explains the asymmetry that makes official responses useless: a denial published once loses to a claim published a hundred times by a hundred people. answer.exemplar: A verdict establishes one thing: that a specific claim, in the words in which it was made and at a stated time, is not supported by the evidence. And it covers no neighbouring claim, which is the trap that causes the most trouble: the same words travel with a different year, a different place, a different subject or a different quantifier, and a verdict on one version does not follow to the next. A verdict is not a judgement of the person who repeated the claim, since repeating something false is not the same as inventing it. And the fact-check is itself a text with a date, so a verdict about last year's claim belongs to the evidence available then and not to what is known now. A verdict of wahr is narrower still, since it can mean only that no evidence contradicts the claim.

The other three options each name a real feature of meetings and then misjudge it. Muted microphones are the correct default in a large meeting, and muting is a courtesy rather than a breach. Formal clothes are a matter of the workplace rather than of the norm, and a room in which somebody is quietly taking notes is not the problem. The last option is simply a different fault, and the fault here is silence.
questions.hint: Ask how the other participants can tell the difference between listening and being absent.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: What a plan for digitale Bildung actually names
questions.learningObjective: set out the three abilities in a plan for digital education and what it leaves unstated

stimulus.body: In einer Arbeitsnotiz zu diesem Punkt heißt es: Vier Aussagen werden angeboten; nur eine wird durch den Text tatsächlich gestützt.

questions.stem: Mit dem Hinweis «set out the three abilities in a plan for digital education and what it leaves unstated / Ask what a pupil can do afterwards that…»: welche Option wird vom Text wirklich gedeckt?

answer.exemplar: The phrase normally names three abilities and leaves the largest part to somebody else. Medienkompetenz covers judging a source, a claim and a post, and it is the ability that survives a change of platform, since the tools change and the questions do not. Datenschutzbewusstsein covers knowing what a service learns about a person and what a single setting actually changes, which is a different question from whether a device is secure. Technische Sicherheit covers passwords, backups, updates and a second factor. Two things are usually missing. The first is any statement about what pupils are to do with a tool, how a teacher plans a lesson with one, and what happens when a service disappears, none of which is a pupil ability and all of which decide whether the three above are ever taught. The second is any statement about checking whether the plan works, and that is the difference between a list of intentions and a programme. The test worth applying is to ask what a pupil can do after the course that they could not do before, since a plan written only in nouns cannot answer that, and to ask what happens to the plan when the tool it names is withdrawn.
